title: Ensemble-dependent condensate statistics and correlations in an ideal Bose gas
authors: Szymon Augustynowicz, Jan Okoński, Maciej B. Kruk, Ilja Zebergs, Jan Joachim Arlt, Kazimierz Rzążewski, Krzysztof Pawłowski
abstract: The choice of statistical ensemble has a measurable impact on the statistical description of Bose-Einstein condensates beyond the well-known grand canonical anomaly. We develop a segmented-contour approach for the ideal Bose gas, which refines the saddle-point approximation by including non-Gaussian corrections in the canonical and microcanonical ensembles. The method applies to a broad class of noninteracting spectra, and provides efficient access to condensate fluctuations, higher moments, and correlation functions.   For a three-dimensional harmonic trap with fixed anisotropy, we find that the ratio of the maxima of the microcanonical and canonical condensate-number variances approaches the theoretically predicted asymptotic value $1-3ζ(3)^2/[4ζ(2)ζ(4)]\approx 0.391$ only extremely slowly with increasing particle number. We also show that ensemble effects are visible in the second-order correlation function $g^{(2)}(x)$ near the condensation crossover. After ballistic release from a three-dimensional harmonic trap, the time evolution of $g^{(2)}(x)$ preserves the differences between statistical ensembles.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the statistical description of ideal Bose-Einstein condensates by rigorously comparing results from the microcanonical, canonical, and grand canonical ensembles. Using a refined segmented-contour method, the authors demonstrate that ensemble choice significantly impacts higher-order correlation functions and fluctuations, even in the thermodynamic limit.
main_problem: The paper investigates how the choice of statistical ensemble (Microcanonical, Canonical, Grand Canonical) measurably affects the statistical description of Bose-Einstein condensates beyond standard equivalence theorems.
main_result: Ensemble effects are visible in higher-order correlation functions like g^(2)(x), and the ratio of condensate-number variances approaches a specific asymptotic value very slowly with increasing particle number.
method: The authors develop and apply a segmented-contour approach to refine the saddle-point approximation, allowing for the inclusion of non-Gaussian corrections in the canonical and microcanonical ensembles.
model_or_system: The system studied is the ideal Bose gas, modeled within a three-dimensional harmonic trap. The analysis compares results derived from the MCE, CE, and GCE frameworks.
key_observables: Condensate-number fluctuations (variances), second-order correlation function g^(2)(x), and the ratio of maximal microcanonical to canonical condensate-number variances.
important_parameters: The analysis focuses on the crossover regime near condensation and the particle number N, which dictates the slow approach to the asymptotic ratio.
main_assumptions: The primary mathematical tools involve refining the saddle-point approximation via segmented contours, and the analysis is initially restricted to the ideal gas limit.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares single realizations of condensate occupation (n0) across GCE, CE, and MCE ensembles, showing distinct statistical scatter, especially below the critical temperature.
paper_structure: The paper develops the mathematical framework by relating the partition functions of the different ensembles, addressing the failure of naive saddle-point approximations due to the ground-state contribution. It then applies this refined method to calculate observables like variances and correlation functions for the trapped ideal Bose gas.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it delves into the subtle, non-trivial differences between statistical ensembles for interacting or near-critical quantum systems, which is a key theoretical challenge in modern quantum many-body physics.
